::: {#thm-tree-paths}
#### A tree has exactly one path between two vertices

Let $G$ be a graph (@def-graph-vertices-edges) with no loops (@def-graph-loop).
Then $G$ is a tree (@def-tree) if and only if,
for every two vertices $u$ and $v$ of $G$, there is exactly one path (@def-graph-path) from $u$ to $v$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

**A tree has exactly one path between two vertices.**
Let $G$ be a tree, and let $u$ and $v$ be vertices of $G$.
Since $G$ is connected (@def-connected), there is a walk from $u$ to $v$,
so there is a path from $u$ to $v$, by @thm-walk-path.

Suppose, for contradiction (@def-proof-by-contradiction), that there are two different paths from $u$ to $v$,
written by their vertices (@rem-tree-simple) as

$$
\ba
u &= p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_m = v,
\\ u &= q_0, q_1, \ldots, q_k = v.
\ea
$$

If $p_j = q_j$ for every $j \le \min(m, k)$, the paths are the same:
if $m < k$, then $q_m = p_m = v = q_k$ would repeat a vertex of the second path,
and $k < m$ is ruled out in the same way.
So there is a smallest $j \ge 1$ with $p_j \ne q_j$.
Let $i = j - 1$, so that $p_i = q_i$ and $p_{i + 1} \ne q_{i + 1}$.

The vertex $p_m = v = q_k$ of the first path is one of $q_{i + 1}, \ldots, q_k$.
Let $a > i$ be the smallest index for which $p_a$ is one of $q_{i + 1}, \ldots, q_k$, say $p_a = q_b$ with $b > i$.
Then

$$
p_i, p_{i + 1}, \ldots, p_a = q_b, q_{b - 1}, \ldots, q_{i + 1}, q_i = p_i
$$

is a closed walk from $p_i$ to itself.
Its vertices before the last one are all different:
$p_i, \ldots, p_a$ are vertices of a path, and so are $q_{b - 1}, \ldots, q_{i + 1}, q_i$;
by the choice of $a$, none of $p_{i + 1}, \ldots, p_{a - 1}$ is one of $q_{i + 1}, \ldots, q_{b - 1}$;
$p_a = q_b$ is not one of $q_{i + 1}, \ldots, q_{b - 1}$;
and $p_i = q_i$ is not one of $q_{i + 1}, \ldots, q_{b - 1}$.
Its length is $(a - i) + (b - i) \ge 3$,
since both terms are at least 1, and $a = b = i + 1$ would give $p_{i + 1} = q_{i + 1}$.
Each edge of the closed walk joins two consecutive vertices,
and since there are at least three vertices before the last one, all different,
no two of these pairs of consecutive vertices are the same set.
So the edges are all different, and the closed walk is a cycle (@def-graph-cycle),
which contradicts that $G$ is a tree.
So there is exactly one path from $u$ to $v$.

**A graph with exactly one path between every two vertices is a tree.**
Suppose that $G$ has no loops and exactly one path between every two vertices.
A path is a walk, so $G$ is connected.
Suppose, for contradiction, that $G$ has a cycle $v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n$, with $v_n = v_0$.
Then $n \ge 2$, since a cycle of length 1 is a loop.
Both

$$
\ba
& v_0, e_1, v_1,
\\ & v_0, e_n, v_{n - 1}, e_{n - 1}, \ldots, e_2, v_1
\ea
$$

are paths from $v_0$ to $v_1$, since the vertices $v_0, \ldots, v_{n - 1}$ of the cycle are all different.
They are different paths:
if $n \ge 3$, the first has length 1 and the second has length $n - 1 \ge 2$,
and if $n = 2$, they use the edges $e_1$ and $e_2$, which are different since a cycle is a trail (@def-trail).
This contradicts that there is exactly one path from $v_0$ to $v_1$.
So $G$ has no cycles, and $G$ is a tree.

:::
